audience: Students with basic programming knowledge learning assembly

progression.localImplementation: Native prose, public intermediate and final CLI checks; remote lesson runner and enforced policies remain pending

title: Compute a SHA-256 fingerprint
prerequisites: Byte intervals, word widths and byte order
Preserved registers, nested calls and stack frames
Explicit streaming state and bounded file reads
learningObjectives: Decode a big-endian block into numeric schedule words
Trace schedule expansion, rounds and feed-forward
Distinguish word arithmetic from full pointers and length counters
Maintain independent contexts over arbitrary update splits
Choose correct one-block or two-block final padding
Publish a complete digest only after successful EOF
Separate simulated instruction work from host latency

steps.title: Identify the message being hashed

quiz.prompt: Is a trailing newline included automatically in this message?

choices.text: No; only the declared input bytes belong to it.
Yes, every text message ends with one.
Only when the digest begins with a high bit.

hints.text: List the selected bytes rather than their visual appearance.
A fourth byte changes the message and therefore the expected digest.

steps.title: Inspect the caller and unfinished exits

quiz.prompt: May a development return be treated as a correct digest?

choices.text: Yes, if output happens to contain zeros.
No; it explicitly marks incomplete work.
Only for an empty file.

hints.text: Trace the branch in the first empty region.
Inspect status before interpreting any output array.

steps.title: Keep a schedule destination and decode count

quiz.prompt: Which pointer must be word-aligned?

choices.text: The source byte pointer.
The schedule destination.
Both pointers must be identical.

hints.text: Separate a byte sequence from a numeric word array.
The later sw instruction addresses the schedule, not the source.

steps.title: Place the first two bytes in their word fields

quiz.prompt: What does shifting the first byte by 24 accomplish?

choices.text: It selects the next input byte.
It changes the source memory order.
It places that byte in the most significant field of the numeric word.

hints.text: Trace one byte before considering the full block.
The byte 61 becomes the word pattern 61000000.

steps.title: Complete and store one decoded word

quiz.prompt: Why is lbu used for the final source byte?

choices.text: A signed final byte could set higher fields during OR.
It swaps every pair of bytes.
It writes the schedule automatically.

hints.text: Consider a final byte with value 80.
A signed byte load would create ones above bit seven.

steps.title: Decode the remaining fifteen words

quiz.prompt: Why does the source advance by four?

choices.text: Each schedule word consumes four source bytes.
There are four compression rounds.
The byte count is stored in words.

hints.text: Relate one loop iteration to one destination word.
Sixteen groups of four bytes consume the entire 64-byte block.

steps.title: Compute small sigma zero from its predecessor

quiz.prompt: Which word is sixty bytes before W16?

hints.text: Count fifteen word-sized steps backward.
Each step is four bytes.

steps.title: Compute small sigma one independently

quiz.prompt: Which operation fills shifted-in bits with zeros?

choices.text: sra.
drotr.
srl.

hints.text: A rotate puts removed bits back into the word.
The non-rotating term in this equation requires a logical word shift.

steps.title: Write each expanded schedule word

quiz.prompt: What may influence an expanded schedule word?

choices.text: The old contents of unused workspace.
The earlier words named by the recurrence.
The file descriptor.

hints.text: Follow the write order from W0 onward.
Every predecessor must have been produced during this call.

steps.title: Check the entire schedule before calling compression

quiz.prompt: What does checking only W0 establish?

choices.text: That all sixty-four rounds are correct.
That every predecessor offset is correct.
Only that one decoded word is correct.

hints.text: Expansion has not contributed to W0.
Test a recurrence result as well as directly decoded values.

steps.title: Call the schedule builder without losing the caller

quiz.prompt: Why reload the state pointer after the nested call?

choices.text: Argument and temporary registers are not preserved by that call.
A schedule is stored in the text segment.
The state pointer must become a word value.

hints.text: Read which registers the schedule loop uses.
The frame retains full addresses in eight-byte slots.

steps.title: Copy the incoming state into working registers

quiz.prompt: Why retain the incoming state words in memory?

choices.text: They are used again in the final feed-forward sums.
They contain the file path.
They are the schedule destination.

hints.text: Distinguish the working vector from the running hash state.
The next state adds the final working vector to the old state.

steps.title: Form capital sigma one of old e

quiz.prompt: Which value supplies all three rotations?

choices.text: The new e after its replacement.
The old e in s4.
The byte count.

hints.text: The right-hand side of a round uses only its old vector.
No working register has been reassigned yet.

steps.title: Add choice, old h, the constant and the schedule word

quiz.prompt: What does a one bit of e select in choice?

choices.text: The corresponding bit of f.
The corresponding bit of g.
The next constant.

hints.text: Think about one bit position at a time.
Use the factored expression g XOR (e AND (f XOR g)).

steps.title: Form capital sigma zero of old a

quiz.prompt: Which temporary must survive this calculation?

choices.text: The already computed T1.
The original source byte in a0.
The current syscall number.

hints.text: Identify the values needed by both new a and new e.
T1 is used twice in the working-vector replacement.

steps.title: Add the majority term to finish T2

quiz.prompt: When is one bit of majority equal to one?

choices.text: Only when all three input bits are one.
When exactly one input bit is one.
When at least two input bits are one.

hints.text: Check the three possible pairs of inputs.
Any pair of ones establishes the majority at that position.

steps.title: Replace the working vector in dependency order

quiz.prompt: What goes wrong if g is overwritten before h receives old g?

choices.text: The old g value can be lost.
The source address becomes aligned.
The round counter increases.

hints.text: Trace two adjacent assignments with distinct bit patterns.
A move copies the register's current value, not its value at the start of the round.

steps.title: Advance constants and schedule entries together

quiz.prompt: How many constants does one block consume?

choices.text: Sixteen.
Sixty-four.
One per input byte including padding twice.

hints.text: There is one Kt in each round equation.
The schedule and constant arrays each contain one word per round.

steps.title: Add the working vector back to the incoming state

quiz.prompt: Which pair is added for the first output state word?

choices.text: Old state word zero and final working a.
Initial a and initial b.
The first two schedule words.

hints.text: Locate the feed-forward step after the round loop.
The final working vector is only one term of the next state.

steps.title: Compare a round boundary and the complete block result

quiz.prompt: Should s0 still hold working a after the function returns?

choices.text: Yes, saved registers are the digest output.
No; the public function restores the caller's s0.
Only when a is negative.

hints.text: The state output is in caller memory.
The internal register allocation is distinct from the function's preserved-register obligation.

steps.title: Install the initial eight-word state

quiz.prompt: Must initialization clear the entire schedule workspace?

choices.text: Yes, every word must initially be zero.
No; later schedule construction writes every word it uses.
Only when a file is opened.

hints.text: Separate meaningful context fields from scratch storage.
An old workspace value must never be needed to build a new schedule.

steps.title: Reset the original length and incomplete-buffer count

quiz.prompt: Why clear eight bytes at context offset thirty-two?

choices.text: It is the full 64-bit byte counter.
The next source byte is eight bytes long.
The schedule contains eight words.

hints.text: A reused context may contain a nonzero upper count word.
A four-byte store would leave half of the counter untouched.

steps.title: Count the supplied message bytes once

quiz.prompt: What does this count include?

choices.text: Only bytes returned by the final read.
All original message bytes supplied across updates.
Padding and schedule bytes.

hints.text: The counter survives more than one update call.
Finalization converts this original-byte count to bits without incrementing it for padding.

steps.title: Guard the source before copying a byte

quiz.prompt: Which check must precede the source load?

choices.text: Whether any input bytes remain.
Whether the output digest is zero.
Whether the source address is word-aligned.

hints.text: A zero-length interval permits no byte load.
The source need not point to readable data for an empty update.

steps.title: Recognize when the buffer becomes full

quiz.prompt: Why not immediately copy byte sixty-five into the same buffer?

choices.text: It would exceed the 64-byte buffer.
It would make the message odd-length.
It would alter the constant table automatically.

hints.text: The buffer occupies context bytes forty-eight through one hundred eleven.
The next context field begins at byte one hundred twelve.

steps.title: Compress the complete buffer

quiz.prompt: Which pointer supplies the compression state?

choices.text: The context base.
The source pointer after its increment.
The digest destination.

hints.text: The eight state words are the first field of the context.
The block buffer and schedule are at separate offsets from that same base.

steps.title: Begin a fresh buffer after compression

quiz.prompt: Which value must be cleared after a full block?

choices.text: The original total.
The used count.
The running eight-word state.

hints.text: A new buffer begins, but the message continues.
Resetting the state would discard all previously compressed blocks.

steps.title: Compare one update with several updates

quiz.prompt: Which context bytes must represent the same tail?

choices.text: The entire unused schedule.
Only the used buffer prefix.
Every byte ever used by any earlier call.

hints.text: The used count establishes which buffer bytes have meaning.
Scratch storage beyond the prefix is not part of the logical tail.

steps.title: Record the bit length and append the marker

quiz.prompt: Does appending 80 increase the original message length?

choices.text: Yes, by one byte.
Yes, by eight bytes.
No; the recorded length excludes padding.

hints.text: Distinguish the bytes sent by the caller from bytes added by finalization.
The length field describes only the original input.

steps.title: Choose whether padding needs an extra block

quiz.prompt: What is the working used count after marking a 56-byte tail?

choices.text: Fifty-six.
Fifty-seven.
Sixty-four.

hints.text: The marker consumes one buffer byte.
Add one before applying the room-for-length test.

steps.title: Finish a block that has no room for the length

quiz.prompt: Where will the length be written on this path?

choices.text: In another block.
Over the last message bytes.
Into the constant table.

hints.text: There were fewer than eight free bytes after the marker.
This block must be compressed before a fresh zero-filled block is completed.

steps.title: Compress the first padding block and restart its count

quiz.prompt: May the final block reuse the same 64-byte storage?

choices.text: No, each block needs a separate allocation.
Yes, after the previous block has been consumed.
Only for ASCII input.

hints.text: Compression has already incorporated the previous block into state.
Reuse storage while preserving the logical sequence of blocks.

steps.title: Leave exactly eight bytes for the length

quiz.prompt: Why stop the fill at index fifty-six?

choices.text: The remaining eight positions hold the length.
Only fifty-six input bytes are allowed.
The schedule has fifty-six words.

hints.text: The block is sixty-four bytes long.
Subtract the eight-byte length field from that capacity.

steps.title: Serialize every bit of the saved length

quiz.prompt: Which width is required for these variable shifts?

choices.text: Eight bits.
Thirty-two bits.
Sixty-four bits.

hints.text: The length field itself occupies sixty-four bits.
Its first extraction shifts by fifty-six, which a word shift cannot express as intended.

steps.title: Consume the complete final block

quiz.prompt: What must happen before writing the digest bytes?

choices.text: The final block must be compressed.
The original total must be reset.
The file must be reopened.

hints.text: The length field contributes to the hash through this block.
A correct padding buffer is not itself the final digest.

steps.title: Publish thirty-two big-endian digest bytes

quiz.prompt: Why not use sw directly on the output?

choices.text: The output has to hold decimal text.
The required byte order differs from a little-endian word store.
A digest word is sixty-four bytes long.

hints.text: Compare numeric ba7816bf with its required bytes ba 78 16 bf.
A little-endian word store would put bf first.

steps.title: Test both sides of the padding boundary

quiz.prompt: How many padding blocks follow an exact 64-byte message?

choices.text: Zero.
One.
Two because the input was full.

hints.text: Update has consumed the message block already.
A fresh block still records the marker and original length.

steps.title: Acquire the supplied file descriptor

quiz.prompt: Which descriptor should later reads use?

choices.text: A fixed value of three.
The nonnegative value returned by open.
The scratch address.

hints.text: The operating environment chooses the descriptor.
Preserve that result across all nested hash calls.

steps.title: Start one fresh hash for this file

quiz.prompt: How often is initialization performed for a file?

choices.text: Before every read.
Only after EOF.
Once before its first read.

hints.text: Read boundaries divide transport, not messages.
All positive reads contribute to one running context.

steps.title: Request a bounded scratch prefix

quiz.prompt: Which bytes in scratch are new input?

choices.text: Every byte up to the capacity.
Only the number reported by the positive result.
Every byte that happens to be nonzero.

hints.text: The buffer may retain older bytes after the returned prefix.
The return value defines the valid input interval.

steps.title: Separate read errors, EOF and positive input

quiz.prompt: What does a positive short read mean here?

choices.text: The returned bytes are valid and another read is needed.
The complete file has ended.
The hash must restart.

hints.text: Only zero denotes EOF in this interface.
The amount returned may be smaller than the amount requested.

steps.title: Hash exactly the returned read count

quiz.prompt: Why copy v0 into the length argument first?

choices.text: It is the actual successful read count.
It is always equal to the capacity.
It contains the expected digest.

hints.text: Nested functions may replace v0.
Retain the syscall result before entering the hash routine.

steps.title: Continue reading until a terminal result

quiz.prompt: Does the hash depend on the number of read calls?

choices.text: Yes, every read adds padding.
No, only the ordered byte sequence contributes.
Only if the capacity is odd.

hints.text: The update function never adds final padding.
Read boundaries disappear at the context interface.

steps.title: Publish only after successful EOF and close

quiz.prompt: When is the output a digest of this complete file?

choices.text: After any positive read.
When scratch is full.
After EOF and successful finalization, with status zero.

hints.text: A partial prefix may not be the entire file.
The caller must inspect status before interpreting output bytes.

steps.title: Distinguish ordinary files from controlled read tests

quiz.prompt: Does an ordinary small file force a read-error branch?

choices.text: Yes, if its length is not a multiple of sixty-four.
No; the error must be exercised deliberately.
Only when the filename contains digits.

hints.text: File contents and transport failures are separate test inputs.
Controlled fixtures make otherwise hard-to-repeat outcomes observable.

steps.title: Exercise equivalent code and independent contexts

quiz.prompt: What must an equivalent implementation preserve?

choices.text: The observable interface and memory contract.
Every temporary register value used by this illustration.
The same source labels inside its loop.

hints.text: Separate an internal teaching checkpoint from a public return boundary.
The caller relies on results and ownership, not the chosen expression for choice.

steps.title: Measure the change at a fixed boundary

quiz.prompt: Do fewer simulated instructions establish lower host elapsed time?

choices.text: Always, with the same numerical ratio.
No; host time requires a separate measurement.
Only when the file is missing.

hints.text: Identify exactly what the counter records.
Session creation, host execution costs and file latency are outside these instruction counts.
